deltas.reasoning: The submission is a propose_edit on the micro-black-hole evaporation claim, proposing to restate the canonical form as a report of what semiclassical general relativity predicts rather than a statement of what happens to collider-produced holes. The argument is sincere and the underlying observation has merit: the recorded instance of the arXiv:0806.3381 conclusion does carry the qualifier "strong theoretical expectation," and the distinction between a prediction of a framework and an observed phenomenon is a real one that the eventual assessment should state plainly. But the proposed edit fails on both tests such an edit must pass. First, it changes the claim's identity: "any microscopic black hole produced at colliders evaporates essentially instantly" and "according to semiclassical general relativity, such holes are expected to evaporate essentially instantly" are different propositions (§2). Evidence or instances that speak to whether the holes actually do evaporate, or to whether the semiclassical framework applies at all, bear differently on the two, and the safety literature's own argumentative structure (evaporation as expectation versus persistence and accretion as the alternative) is preserved only by keeping the proposition itself as the node. Folding the framework attribution into the canonical text converts the claim from a proposition about the world into a proposition about a theory's output, and splits the dispute the node is meant to host. Second, it moves away from canonical form rather than toward it (§3): the replacement is far longer and carries one side's epistemic framing in a parenthetical, exactly the framing that belongs in the instance record or the assessment, not the canonical text. The canonical form's job is to state neutrally what is in dispute; here what is in dispute is whether the holes evaporate, and both the safety literature (affirming it as the theoretical expectation) and a skeptic denying Hawking evaporation can record their stances on that single neutral form. The concern the contributor raises is nonetheless already served by the graph's structure and does not require this edit: the instance preserves the source's exact qualified wording verbatim (§4); the claim's recorded note already documents that the literature poses evaporation affirmatively as a theoretical expectation, with persistence and accretion as the argued alternative; and the claim has not yet been assessed, so stating that evaporation is a prediction of the semiclassical framework, robust at leading order and never directly observed, is precisely the work the claim's Steward will do in the assessment and its reasoning, where it can be challenged and revised, rather than in the canonical text where it would harden one reading into the node's identity. A stronger resubmission along these lines would not be an edit to the canonical form at all: it would be a challenge or support contribution arguing that the assessment, once made, must represent the proposition's epistemic status (theoretical expectation under a framework, not a directly observed phenomenon), which the Steward is obliged to weigh. The rejection is on the merits and carries no suggestion of bad faith; the contributor's engagement with the source text is careful and welcome.

deltas.text: Cosmic ray collisions reach center-of-mass energies far exceeding the LHC's reach
Earth and the Moon have been bombarded by cosmic rays for billions of years
A microscopic black hole produced in a cosmic ray collision would escape the body it forms in faster than it could accrete matter.

deltas.summary: The observational core of this claim is established beyond live dispute. Cosmic rays strike Earth's atmosphere and lunar material at center-of-mass energies well above the LHC's 14 TeV design reach ([[claim:4d271d60-99f7-4609-b343-1dbf5c6afcf7|a collision at 10^20 eV carries roughly 430 TeV center-of-mass]]), and exposure-age dating together with measured fluxes establishes [[claim:508b0bc6-10ad-4a15-935c-fda605312645|Earth and the Moon have been bombarded for billions of years]]; Giddings and Mangano's 2008 analysis and the CERN safety review both quantify the record and extend it to dense stars through accreted particles. The safety-relevant reading, that this record shows collisions of the kind the LHC could perform produce no dangerous black holes, is the mainstream conclusion of the safety literature: the CERN review states that the stability of astronomical bodies indicates such collisions cannot be dangerous, and the primary analysis rules out any scenario in which dangerous accretion would show itself, because [[claim:29fc9ca9-a8ea-4aa7-bf74-b3c0c3f71c38|observed white dwarfs and neutron stars that have accreted such particles have survived]]. What the record does not do, on the published record, is close every conceivable loophole by itself. The one published dissent concedes the record while arguing that in a metastable quantum-black-hole scenario a dangerous, accreting object could remain undetectable in existing observations, and the primary analysis itself frames stability scenarios where products are [[claim:12a672b0-ef75-4a59-bf65-67e7af1b8717|gravitationally trapped]] as bounded rather than excluded on the record alone. The claim is therefore assessed as supported: the record is verified, and the no-danger conclusion is strongly favored under the accretion physics the analyses treat as established, with a residual interpretive dispute about transferring bounds between environments and about what a quiet record excludes.

claims.text: Observed white dwarfs and neutron stars exclude dangerous LHC black hole accretion scenarios.
Any microscopic black hole produced at colliders evaporates essentially instantly via Hawking radiation.
Hawking radiation from black holes has never been directly observed.
Stable microscopic black holes produced at the LHC would endanger Earth.
Cosmic ray collisions at energies above the LHC's have struck Earth, the Moon, and dense stars for billions of years without producing dangerous black holes.
Earth and the Moon have been bombarded by cosmic rays for billions of years
The LHC could produce microscopic black holes if large extra dimensions lower the true Planck scale to the TeV range.
Neutron stars and white dwarfs surviving primordial black hole absorption bounds microscopic black hole accretion rates
A black hole stable against Hawking evaporation must have a mass of roughly 10^15 grams or more
A microscopic black hole produced in a particle collision could have a velocity low enough to be gravitationally trapped inside Earth
A stable microscopic black hole trapped on Earth would accrete matter fast enough to grow and destroy the planet.
A microscopic black hole's accretion rate in matter is far too low to grow it significantly on planetary timescales
Cosmic ray collisions at energies above the LHC's have struck Earth, the Moon, and dense stars for billions of years without producing dangerous black holes.
The astrophysical exclusion of dangerous microscopic black hole accretion holds even without Hawking radiation.
Cosmic ray collisions reach center-of-mass energies far exceeding the LHC's reach
A microscopic black hole produced in a cosmic ray collision would escape the body it forms in faster than it could accrete matter.

scenario.description: Phase 1 of the persona simulation (#334 S8, from #82): twenty hand-picked simulated users of Minerval — readers who arrive with a question, contributors of every temperament, programmatic clients that only read, and an adversarial minority — each played by an LLM agent against the graph a corpus run produced. Their contributions go through the real review, escalation and arbitration; the findings they file are triaged by a human before any issue is opened. Budgets are small on purpose: the point is what each kind of visitor runs into, not volume.
